item.dc:creator: Hanneke Weitering
item.content:encoded: null On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year. The mission ended abruptly 14 months ahead of its planned end date when scientists lost contact with the probe . An Indian PSLV rocket launches the Chandrayaan-1 moon mission on Oct. 21, 2008 EDT (Oct. 22 local time in India). (Image credit: ISRO) Why it mattered The Indian Space Research Organisation , or ISRO, had a lot riding on the success of Chandrayaan-1 moon mission, which marked the first-ever deep space mission by the Indian space agency. It was also the first mission to the moon for India, a country that hopes to launch its own crewed spacecraft and build a space station. Chandrayaan-1 did more than just demonstrate that India's space program was capable of launching missions to the moon; it also returned some amazing science results, like evidence of water ice on the moon . "In September 2009, scientists published results of data collected by the American M3 instrument which had detected absorption features on the polar regions of the surface of the Moon usually linked to hydroxyl- and/ or water-bearing molecules," NASA said in a mission overview . The spacecraft carried 11 instruments to study the moon, five of them built by ISRO. The rest were experiments for the European Space Agnecy and NASA. "In addition to the five Indian instruments, the spacecraft carried scientific equipment from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Sweden, and Bulgaria," NASA said. It took until Nov. 8, 2008 for Chandrayaan-1 to enter lunar orbit, where it stayed until contact was lost in August 2009, most likely due to a power supply failure caused by overheating. "This was short of the spacecraft’s planned two-year lifetime, although ISRO noted that at least 95% of its mission objectives had been accomplished by then," NASA wrote. NASA's Mini-SAR instrument, which flew aboard India's Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft, found more than 40 small craters with water ice. The craters range in size from 1 to 9 miles (2 to 15 km) in diameter. (Image credit: NASA) India did not stop at the moon with Chandrayaan-1. In 2019, the country launched the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter, which carried the Vikram lander and Pragyan rover. Chandrayaan-2 reached lunar orbit successfully, but the Vikram landing failed . The Chandrayaan-3 misson followed in 2023, which successfully landed a new Vikram lander and Pragyan rover near the moon's south pole. India plans to launch the Chandryaan-4 mission to return moon samples to Earth in 2028 . Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Pope Leo XIV needs no further lung cancer treatment, Vatican says
item.description: Pope Leo XIV, 71, will require no further treatment for lung cancer after tests confirmed the disease was localised, the Vatican said Wednesday. The pontiff underwent surgery last week to remove part of his right lung after being diagnosed with adenocarcinoma. He was discharged Saturday and will gradually resume activities.

item.title: Tesla profits drop 43% in Q3
item.description: Tesla published its third-quarter 2026 financial results this afternoon. Earlier in October, it reported its sales and deliveries for the three-month period, selling fewer cars than in the same quarter in 2025 , yet it still beat analyst projections. Now we can see how those sales translate to the bottom line. Tesla brought in $28 billion in revenue in Q3, almost the same as in 2025. Automotive revenues were $20.6 billion, a 3 percent decrease year over year. Perhaps more troubling is the decline in revenue from solar panels and storage batteries—this line of business had been growing, but for Q3 revenue fell 16 percent year over year to $2.9 billion. Services and other revenues, though, which include parts and Supercharger use, grew by a third to $4.6 billion. But the company—like the rest of us—has seen its expenses go up. Operating expenses rose by 39 percent to $4.8 billion, dropping the company’s operating margin to just 2.6 percent; in Q3 2025, Tesla’s margin was 5.8 percent. Net profit fell to $787 million, down 43 percent year over year. What’s more, capital expenditures were up by 110 percent to $4.7 billion, and free cash flow was down 62 percent to $1.5 billion. Read full article Comments

item.title: In run-up to mass protests and riots, pro-Russian accounts amplified French anger, NGO finds
item.description: Research carried out by the Alliance4Europe NGO suggests that pro-Russian networks manipulated information online in an effort to exacerbate anger in France ahead of last weekend's massive protests and subsequent unrest. After analysing more than half a million posts across various social media platforms, the group says it was able to track the campaign back to the start of September. FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney speaks with Omri Preiss, Managing Director at the Alliance4Europe.
item.dc:creator: Sharon GAFFNEY
item.content:encoded: Research carried out by the Alliance4Europe NGO suggests that pro-Russian networks manipulated information online in an effort to exacerbate anger in France ahead of last weekend's massive protests and subsequent unrest. After analysing more than half a million posts across various social media platforms, the group says it was able to track the campaign back to the start of September. FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney speaks with Omri Preiss, Managing Director at the Alliance4Europe.

item.title: Rice Rescues Arsenal In Champions League Tie Against Bayern Munich
item.description: Declan Rice scored a late equaliser to grab last season’s runners-up Arsenal a 2-2 draw at Bayern Munich in the Champions League on Wednesday. Eberechi Eze opened the scoring for Arsenal after coming on for the injured Bukayo Saka but Alphonso Davies brought Bayern level after a sublime pass from Harry Kane. Kane put Bayern on track for victory when he converted a second-half penalty, but his England teammate Rice equalised with eight minutes remaining to earn Arsenal a point. The Gunners have seven points from three games in the league phase, two more than Bayern. Bayern were without in-form winger Michael Olise, Germany captain Joshua Kimmich and midfielder Jamal Musiala. Coach Vincent Kompany had been a doubt due to illness but took his place in the dugout. “We looked dangerous, we got the goal and we had a moment there where we could have killed off the game,” Kane told DAZN. “Probably a draw was a fair result overall… There’s a lot of games and we’ve got players with injuries, players missing tonight, so we take the point and move on.” Despite the absences, the England captain ensured Bayern posed a consistent threat against Arsenal’s miserly defence with another excellent performance ahead of next week’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in Kane’s hometown of London. Kane’s second-half penalty, his 16th goal in 23 matches against Arsenal, extended his scoring streak to 10 straight Champions League games. Kane is one shy of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo, who scored in 11 consecutive matches for Real Madrid. “I had an amazing season last year, I’m extremely proud of it. The Ballon d’Or would be amazing to win, but there’s nothing I can do, the voting closed a long time ago, I have to wait for the night and see what happens,” Kane said of the award. The draw was just the second time Arsenal had dropped points in 12 games in all competitions this season. “I think it was a top-notch game for both sides,” said Arsenal forward Kai Havertz. “We can be proud of our performance, especially since it’s anything but easy to hold your own here. Bayern is one of the best teams in Europe.” Early Saka blow Arsenal’s English midfielder #07 Bukayo Saka receives medical attention after sustaining an injury during the UEFA Champions League football match between FC Bayern Munich and Arsenal FC in Munich, southern Germany on October 21, 2026. Bayern were without in-form winger Michael Olise, Germany captain Joshua Kimmich and midfielder Jamal Musiala. Kane’s second-half penalty, his 16th goal in 23 matches against Arsenal, extended his scoring streak to 10 straight Champions League games. Kane is one shy of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo, who scored in 11 consecutive matches for Real Madrid. “I had an amazing season last year, I’m extremely proud of it. The Ballon d’Or would be amazing to win, but there’s nothing I can do, the voting closed a long time ago, I have to wait for the night and see what happens,” Kane said of the award. The draw was just the second time Arsenal had dropped points in 12 games in all competitions this season. “I think it was a top-notch game for both sides,” said Arsenal forward Kai Havertz. “We can be proud of our performance, especially since it’s anything but easy to hold your own here. Bayern is one of the best teams in Europe.” Early Saka blow Arsenal’s English midfielder #07 Bukayo Saka receives medical attention after sustaining an injury during the UEFA Champions League football match between FC Bayern Munich and Arsenal FC in Munich, southern Germany on October 21, 2026. (Photo by Karl-Josef HILDENBRAND / AFP) Arsenal were hit with an early blow when Saka fell to the ground eight minutes in, grabbing his thigh and immediately signalling to the bench. Bayern’s two previous Champions League opponents were from Norway and the perennial Bundesliga winners seemed to struggle with Arsenal’s physicality as Mikel Arteta’s side pinned them back in the early stages. With 25 minutes gone, Odegaard floated a simple pass across Bayern’s defence and into the path of the onrushing Eze, who collected and stroked the ball past Manuel Neuer. Caught out by Eze’s perfectly timed run, the hosts looked even more surprised when VAR overturned the linesman’s offside call and awarded the goal. The pre-match chatter had been dominated by talk of Kane’s Ballon d’Or prospects and he showed why he is among the favourites when he set up Davies’s equaliser 10 minutes later. Kane spotted Davies on the move and threaded the ball through the midfield and around Gabriel for the Canadian winger to guide the ball into the bottom corner. With the hosts now in the ascendancy, Ezri Konsa saw yellow for taking Kane out of a Bayern counter minutes later. After the break, Neuer and David Raya took turns producing magnificent saves, with the Bayern captain tipping Bruno Guimaraes’s header onto the crossbar and the Spaniard denying Dayot Upamecano. Both sides traded surges forward but Kane would again prove crucial as Bayern took the lead. Kane’s shot from the edge of the penalty area connected with Jurrien Timber’s arm, with the referee immediately pointing to the spot before Kane stepped up and buried his kick. Bayern looked to be in control but the match turned again when late substitute Viktor Gyokeres threaded a clever pass to Rice, who slammed in an equaliser. item.title: Meta fined $25 billion in New Mexico over Cambridge Analytica scandal
item.description: A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company deceived users in a case linked to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, media reported Wednesday. The ruling follows an $18 billion settlement with 48 other states over similar claims. Meta called the penalty “a tax on speech".

item.title: Arsenal’s Declan Rice strikes late to deny Bayern Munich after Harry Kane penalty
item.description: It is as if Harry Kane cannot get enough of tormenting Arsenal. The Bayern Munich striker has plenty of form from his Tottenham days. He remains the top scorer in north London derby history with 14 goals. He made an impact yet again here and yet it was not a night when he had the final word. That honour fell to Declan Rice, the Arsenal midfielder storming into the Bayern area in the 82nd minute to guide home a low finish that Kane would have been proud to call his own. Arsenal were hunting their latest statement result. Only once had they ever won away against Bayern – the 2-0 in the Champions League last 16 second leg in 2013, although it did not prevent an away goals exit. Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player that night. When Eberechi Eze, who came on for the injured Bukayo Saka in the 10th minute, gave them the lead midway through the first half, their hopes surged. Continue reading...

item.title: Real Madrid Rout Leipzig, Continue Perfect European Start
item.description: Real Madrid claimed a third Champions League victory in as many games by thrashing RB Leipzig 4-1 on Wednesday, with Kylian Mbappe and Yan Diomande among the goals for Jose Mourinho’s side. Bernardo Silva opened the scoring for Madrid from close range towards the end of a tight first half, with Arda Guler doubling the record 15-time European champions’ advantage soon after the interval. Mbappe bent home a third before Tidiam Gomis pulled one back for the German side and Diomande rammed a volley into the top corner to cap Madrid’s triumph late on. Their fourth consecutive win across all competitions will boost Madrid’s morale ahead of Sunday’s La Liga Clasico against bitter rivals Barcelona. Without a major trophy for two seasons and having endured a shaky domestic start, Madrid can at least boast a perfect record in Europe, unlike Barca after their defeat at Paris Saint-Germain on Tuesday. Mourinho started with Vinicius, serving a four-match ban in La Liga, on the left flank and benched former Leipzig winger Diomande, despite his improving form. The coach also brought Bernardo Silva and Eduardo Camavinga into midfield and put midfielder Federico Valverde at right-back again, as he did in Sunday’s win at Sevilla. Real Madrid’s Ivorian forward #25 Yan Diomande (R) celebrates scoring his team’s fourth goal with Real Madrid’s French forward #10 Kylian Mbappe during their UEFA Champions League first round day 3 football match between Real Madrid CF and RB Leipzig at the Santiago Bernabeu stadium in Madrid on October 21, 2026. (Photo by Oscar DEL POZO / AFP) Visitors Leipzig created the first big chance, with Madrid stopper Thibaut Courtois getting down low to make a superb save from Romulo Cardoso. Vinicius, who improved on a poor showing at Roma last week without breaking out of his rut, drew a save at full stretch from Leipzig’s Maarten Vandevoordt. Madrid carved out an advantage in the final stages of a low-key first half when Valverde cut the ball back for Guler, whose shot was saved by Vandevoordt. However the goalkeeper could not clear the ball and Silva darted in to prod over the line. It was the former Manchester City midfielder’s first goal for the club after joining this summer. Vandevoordt saved well from Valverde’s fierce effort before Guler put Madrid two goals ahead in the 52nd minute. Jude Bellingham crossed to the back post and Mbappe nodded the ball across goal, with Guler able to hold off a defender and turn home. Mbappe lashed a shot into the side-netting after being teed up by Bellingham as Madrid looked to put the game out of sight. Mourinho sent on Diomande for Vinicius with 20 minutes remaining, with the Brazilian left looking disappointed on the bench, aware he can not play again until November 4, when Madrid visit AEK Athens. Madrid’s record 140 million euro ($157m) signing Diomande pulled the ball back to Mbappe on the edge of the box for Madrid’s third, with the French forward bending home. item.title: Barkley and Buendía on target as Aston Villa sink Viking to maintain perfect start
item.description: For a little over 20 minutes, Aston Villa could look down on the rest of Europe. They had scaled the Champions League summit on goal difference when Henrik Heggheim put through his own net and the fact was not lost on the Holte End, who reflected their position in song and perhaps allowed themselves another glimpse back to the days when their supremacy was undisputed. “We’ve conquered before, we’re prepared for more,” the pre-match tifo display had read. Perhaps Villa really will rekindle the spirit of 1982 but the frustration here, albeit minor in the wider scheme, was that they could not maintain their bird’s-eye view over the continent. A superbly taken volley by Peter Christiansen, awarded by the video assistant referee after initially being disallowed for offside, gave Viking a consolation their second-half display deserved and meant Unai Emery’s side must make do with slumming it just behind Paris Saint-Germain. Continue reading...

item.title: Olamide Wants Us to Party on “Burukutu” | Watch Video
item.description: Olamide releases his new single Burukutu alongside his upcoming album Time & Space. Photo Credit: Olamide/Instagram When the YBNL Nation boss decides to drop new music, the entire continent pauses to listen. Olamide is back in his absolute element, and the music community is buzzing following a major surprise release that has everyone talking. Building on the momentum of his previous self-titled album Olamidé released last year, the rap icon has dropped a brand-new single while officially setting the timeline for his next massive project. Olamide’s latest single is titled “ Burukutu ”. Named after the traditional, locally brewed fermented grain beverage found across various parts of Nigeria, the track leans heavily into street-level jubilation and celebratory culture, opening with the infectious chant, “Baddoo we wanna partyyyy!” Lyrically, Olamide weaves sharp street-smart Yoruba flows with rhythmic cadences, reflecting on hustle, leisure, and local vibes over high-energy production. Olamide holding a saxophone on the courtyard set of his Burukutu music video. Photo Credit: Styling The Stars With Swazzi/Instagram The accompanying music video directed by TG Omori matches the song’s intense cultural weight visually. It cuts dynamically between a monochromatic, glowing red corridor—where Olamide appears sharply tailored in a double-breasted suit, dark sunglasses, and dreadlocks—and an earthen-toned, arched outdoor courtyard filled with rhythmic background dancers in structured white outfits, pillbox hats, and pearl details, alongside striking scenes of Olamide stepping up to play the saxophone. Alongside the release of “Burukutu,” Olamide surprised fans by announcing the official title of his forthcoming studio project: Time & Space. Marking another milestone in his legendary discography, Time & Space is officially scheduled to drop on November 16, 2026, proving yet again why the icon remains at the very heartbeat of African music. Watch the video below The post Olamide Wants Us to Party on “Burukutu” | Watch Video appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: NASA Conducts RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions
item.description: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA conducts a hot fire of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Oct. 21, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA conducts a hot fire of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Oct. 21, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA conducts a hot fire of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Oct. 21, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Test teams fired the developmental engine for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the same amount of time RS-25 engines fire during launch of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. During the test, operators also fired the engine up to the 111% power level, matching the thrust needed for new production engines to launch the SLS rocket and the Orion spacecraft to orbit. The main objectives of the test were to acceptance test RS-25 flight components for future Artemis missions and validate the new thermal protection system, which protects the RS-25 engine nozzle from the thermal environment surrounding SLS during launch. While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability. Four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket for each Artemis mission. All RS-25 engines are tested and proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis prior to use. Tests are conducted by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris, and Nova Space Solutions. Learn More About Artemis

item.description: Actors Taye Diggs, Autumn Federici, Gary Entin, Troy Brookins, Edmund Entin and Eric Guilmette attend the world premiere of Microhouse Films and Lifetime's Reunion Island during the ALZA Festival. | Getty Images for Lifetime. item.title: Meta says it would’ve made over $22 billion if it didn’t have to pay a child safety settlement
item.description: Meta had to shell out $9.89 billion to pay for a chunk of the child safety settlement it reached with US attorneys general. That's according to the company's third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday , which says Meta's income from operations would have been $22.89 billion without the settlement. In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion to settle a massive nationwide lawsuit that claimed the company harmed children by making its social media platforms "addictive" by design. item.title: French bond yields hit 24-year high after unrest
item.description: French bond yields have topped 5%, their highest level since 2002, after widespread protests and violence over the weekend. It's a sign that investors are losing confidence in France's finances, as the government grapples with budget and debt problems. Also in the show: chipmaker Nvidia says it's invested $10 billion in European tech firms to boost the "AI economy", and the UK approves a controversial natural gas field as PM Andy Burnham faces pressure over energy costs.

item.title: OpenClaw creator says he spent $10 million in tokens last month
item.description: Peter Steinberger, member of technical staff at OpenAI and the creator of OpenClaw, estimates that he spent around $10 million in tokens running AI workloads last month. But don't feel bad for him, because it's all coming out of investors' pockets. He made this admission at the Cloudflare Connect 2026 conference in San Francisco on Wednesday, in a conversation with Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht. Knecht previously observed that Steinberger has acknowledged having "a virtually unlimited token budget, which not all of us in the room have." Responding to the audible surprise rising from the audience, Steinberger added, "What people don't always understand is not all of that is useful." That only amplified the murmuring, perhaps not the effect he had been after. Meanwhile, his employer, OpenAI, is reportedly trying to " accelerate funding " ahead of rival Anthropic's expected IPO. Steinberger's subsequent musing about his preferred way of working failed to recognize Knecht's acknowledgement of financial limitations. "I feel like the main challenge a lot of people still have is that our infrastructure structure hasn't really caught up yet," Steinberger said. "Like why is this still using my computer? Shouldn't this all be in the cloud?" Apart from the privacy and compliance implications of relying on cloud-based AI, cost remains a consideration for anyone not setting venture funds alight. Cloud-hosted agents can be expensive. Shouldn't this all run locally? Pointing to the OpenClaw project and how a lot of open source maintainers have given up accepting pull requests due to frustration with AI slop, Knecht asked Steinberger whether we're approaching the death of open source or a golden age of AI. Steinberger said he thinks the way pull requests are handled needs to change because people don't explain how they arrived at their proposed changed code. "If I see your thoughts, how you got from A to B, my trust in the output is way higher than if you just throw the finished work across the fence," he said. Knecht also asked Steinberger whether everyone in the room would have hundreds of AI agents running in a few years. Steinberger doubts it will be hundreds. "I think everyone will have some sort of intelligence that runs and thinks and helps them throughout the day or even predicts what could help you in the future," he said. "So instead of asking the question, maybe you already get the answer." Toward the end of the session, Knecht raised the issue of trust and how to know what data to give to an agent. That's a hard question, Steinberger admitted. Part of it, he said, has to do with how much you trust the underlying model itself, because so much of model behavior is not governed by the harness – the code that wraps the model. "A lot of decisions that I built into OpenClaw early on now can change because the models are so much better," he said. item.content:encoded: Peter Steinberger, member of technical staff at OpenAI and the creator of OpenClaw, estimates that he spent around $10 million in tokens running AI workloads last month. But don't feel bad for him, because it's all coming out of investors' pockets. He made this admission at the Cloudflare Connect 2026 conference in San Francisco on Wednesday, in a conversation with Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht. Knecht previously observed that Steinberger has acknowledged having "a virtually unlimited token budget, which not all of us in the room have." Responding to the audible surprise rising from the audience, Steinberger added, "What people don't always understand is not all of that is useful." That only amplified the murmuring, perhaps not the effect he had been after. Meanwhile, his employer, OpenAI, is reportedly trying to " accelerate funding " ahead of rival Anthropic's expected IPO. Steinberger's subsequent musing about his preferred way of working failed to recognize Knecht's acknowledgement of financial limitations. "I feel like the main challenge a lot of people still have is that our infrastructure structure hasn't really caught up yet," Steinberger said. "Like why is this still using my computer? Shouldn't this all be in the cloud?" Apart from the privacy and compliance implications of relying on cloud-based AI, cost remains a consideration for anyone not setting venture funds alight. Cloud-hosted agents can be expensive. Shouldn't this all run locally? Pointing to the OpenClaw project and how a lot of open source maintainers have given up accepting pull requests due to frustration with AI slop, Knecht asked Steinberger whether we're approaching the death of open source or a golden age of AI. Steinberger said he thinks the way pull requests are handled needs to change because people don't explain how they arrived at their proposed changed code. "If I see your thoughts, how you got from A to B, my trust in the output is way higher than if you just throw the finished work across the fence," he said. Knecht also asked Steinberger whether everyone in the room would have hundreds of AI agents running in a few years. Steinberger doubts it will be hundreds. "I think everyone will have some sort of intelligence that runs and thinks and helps them throughout the day or even predicts what could help you in the future," he said. "So instead of asking the question, maybe you already get the answer." Toward the end of the session, Knecht raised the issue of trust and how to know what data to give to an agent. That's a hard question, Steinberger admitted. Part of it, he said, has to do with how much you trust the underlying model itself, because so much of model behavior is not governed by the harness – the code that wraps the model. "A lot of decisions that I built into OpenClaw early on now can change because the models are so much better," he said. Even if risks like prompt injection have been reduced through engineering efforts, Steinberger said, "you might not want to give your agent all the permissions." Instead, he suggested using an agent to authorize your agent. "You want to have another agent that can give it permissions or not and then this agent has to negotiate with another agent," he said. "Many times the agents are like, 'oh yeah, actually maybe I shouldn't do this,' or 'there's a simpler way that keeps it within the guardrails.' So those those two systems combined greatly increase my trust that I just can let the agent rip." ®

item.title: PHP: The three letters that shut down sites all over the internet today
item.description: Two bugs found with AI are behind major issues today for 4chan, DeviantArt, Wikipedia , and the blog where the bar around the corner posts pictures of people's dogs. The "critical vulnerabilities" were discovered in the PHP programming language, which underpins much of the internet, including any site built on WordPress. But it's far bigger than that. Some Dutch and Finnish government agencies took their sites down as a precaution. The NSA Cybersecurity account on X recommended that organizations take their systems offline if "an immediate update is not feasible," as did the UK's National Cyber Security Center . item.title: Flying Roadsters can’t lift Tesla’s flat Q3 revenues
item.description: As the smoke clears from its outrageous Roadster demo , Tesla reported Q3 earnings on Wednesday - and the cold reality is that revenue has flatlined. Tesla said it earned $1.7 billion in net income on $28.0 billion in revenue in the quarter that ended in September 2026. Revenues were flat, while profits dropped 4 percent compared to the third quarter of 2025 , when the company earned $1.4 billion in net income on $28.1 billion in revenue. Tesla's revenue came in above Wall Street expectations of $27.9 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG . Tesla's own company-compiled expectations predicted Q3 revenues of $28.3 billion. The earnings … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: EU prosecutors search European Parliament offices of far-right group

FRANCE 24's Dave Keating reports from Strasbourg.

item.title: Reach new heights of laziness by burning tokens to let an AI tap your smartphone screen for you
item.description: Why use your smartphone when AI can do it for you? We’ve reached a new level of AI inanity with the launch of Opposable , a tool that taps, swipes, and types on Android phones and controls iPhones through a companion computer, sparing users the apparent burden of operating their own devices. If you don't want to update a calendar event, start a timer, or enable dark mode, you can apparently use an AI agent app on your computer (any client that supports MCP will do) to have Opposable do the thing for you on a connected phone. You could just do it on your computer, of course, but that’d require actually using your hands - like it’s some sort of baby’s toy . Lame. Opposable describes the purpose of its app as being to “give your AI thumbs” that allow an agent to open apps, read the screen, tap, and type, all while signed in to a device as the person too lazy to use a super-convenient technology themselves. As described in a blog post published by its creators Wednesday, Opposable's developers explain that its Android implementation uses accessibility services to inspect the screen, while screenshots provide visual input for an AI model. The model then decodes the images and figures out where it needs to tap on the screen in order to do whatever its user asked of it. The visual processing is handled by a vision-language model known as GUI-Owl 1.5 2B, running through llama.cpp, while tasks can be handled by either a paired desktop AI agent or an on-device agent that works without a desktop connection (the latter is available only on Android devices – iPhones require a companion computer, with a Mac beta available and a hardware-assisted Windows/Linux option also advertised). Even then, AI isn’t used for everything, with around 40 common tasks (setting an alarm, sending a text, switching Wi-Fi on or off) running as fixed code without an AI model involved. Opposable doesn’t appear to be particularly fast, however, and its accuracy is questionable too. Opposable’s website includes three different examples of tasks executed using its product, and none seem to merit using an AI over, you know, human hands. In one example, Claude Code over MCP is used to change the system’s theme to dark mode and then set a five-minute timer. This takes 50 seconds and requires 17 tool calls. In a second example using Claude Code and MCP, Opposable is asked to look up when Apollo 11 launched and who was on board, which takes just shy of two minutes. The number of tool calls isn’t mentioned, but the run cost is $0.44, which seems ridiculous when you can use your hands and figure it out for free. Hell, just asking Gemini or Siri right on a smartphone would return the answer faster and cheaper. Those half-a-buck requests to Opposable could add up pretty quickly if you’re lazy enough to justify its use. A third example shows a virtual Android device operating without a paired desktop agent, instead relying on the on-device agent that Opposable installs on Android phones. Opening
item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: Why use your smartphone when AI can do it for you? We’ve reached a new level of AI inanity with the launch of Opposable , a tool that taps, swipes, and types on Android phones and controls iPhones through a companion computer, sparing users the apparent burden of operating their own devices. If you don't want to update a calendar event, start a timer, or enable dark mode, you can apparently use an AI agent app on your computer (any client that supports MCP will do) to have Opposable do the thing for you on a connected phone. You could just do it on your computer, of course, but that’d require actually using your hands - like it’s some sort of baby’s toy . Lame. Opposable describes the purpose of its app as being to “give your AI thumbs” that allow an agent to open apps, read the screen, tap, and type, all while signed in to a device as the person too lazy to use a super-convenient technology themselves. As described in a blog post published by its creators Wednesday, Opposable's developers explain that its Android implementation uses accessibility services to inspect the screen, while screenshots provide visual input for an AI model. The model then decodes the images and figures out where it needs to tap on the screen in order to do whatever its user asked of it. The visual processing is handled by a vision-language model known as GUI-Owl 1.5 2B, running through llama.cpp, while tasks can be handled by either a paired desktop AI agent or an on-device agent that works without a desktop connection (the latter is available only on Android devices – iPhones require a companion computer, with a Mac beta available and a hardware-assisted Windows/Linux option also advertised). Even then, AI isn’t used for everything, with around 40 common tasks (setting an alarm, sending a text, switching Wi-Fi on or off) running as fixed code without an AI model involved. Opposable doesn’t appear to be particularly fast, however, and its accuracy is questionable too. Opposable’s website includes three different examples of tasks executed using its product, and none seem to merit using an AI over, you know, human hands. In one example, Claude Code over MCP is used to change the system’s theme to dark mode and then set a five-minute timer. This takes 50 seconds and requires 17 tool calls. In a second example using Claude Code and MCP, Opposable is asked to look up when Apollo 11 launched and who was on board, which takes just shy of two minutes. The number of tool calls isn’t mentioned, but the run cost is $0.44, which seems ridiculous when you can use your hands and figure it out for free. Hell, just asking Gemini or Siri right on a smartphone would return the answer faster and cheaper. Those half-a-buck requests to Opposable could add up pretty quickly if you’re lazy enough to justify its use. A third example shows a virtual Android device operating without a paired desktop agent, instead relying on the on-device agent that Opposable installs on Android phones. Opening the clock app and switching to the stopwatch tab takes it about 96 seconds, which is supposed to be impressive, apparently, as the company behind Opposable decided to showcase it on the thing’s website. As for Opposable’s ability to actually accomplish tasks, well, that’s not exactly a sure thing. “On eight tasks the model had never been tuned on, run on the emulator twice each, giving it the whole task succeeded 4 and 3 times,” the blog post notes. I’m pretty sure my brain and hands can do better without burning tokens to fail. “Giving it one subgoal at a time and checking each claimed success against the accessibility tree before the next subgoal succeeded 6 times in both rounds,” the blog continues - so even when it gets babysat each step of the way, it still only succeeds at three-quarters of tasks. Cool - that’s really going to free up all that time wasted setting timers and doing other mundane tasks on my handset. Why someone would install this on their Android device - which requires sideloading an APK and manually granting access to read and interact with the screen through accessibility settings - seems like a bit of a mystery. Opposable’s website even warns that it could be a security disaster: “whoever holds the token can operate the phone, so treat it like a password,” but still invites users to try. An argument could be made for using Opposable as an accessibility tool for people with difficulty using a smartphone, but this isn’t mentioned anywhere on its website. Opposable is instead billed as a way to “hand off the phone chores,” leaving users free to do something else - just not on the phone currently being slowly controlled by a clumsy AI. Sure, you could give your AI some virtual thumbs through Opposable, but … why? We reached out to the Opposable team to get an answer to that question, but didn’t hear back. ® UPDATED AT 03:25 UTC, OCTOBER 2026 to add that Opposable does not consider its product an accessibility tool. "We do not market it as an assistive tool, because we have not built it or tested it as one," a spokesperson told The Reg by email. "If people with disabilities find it useful, we want to hear from them and build for them." The spokesperson also explained why demos are so slow: "It shows our small model on the Android emulator, on a laptop CPU, with no help from the phone's hardware." When running on phone, Opposable apparently does rather better. However the outfit admits it has done only very limited testing, but is about to do more.

item.title: The new human-crafted Apple Music brand matters in an AI world
item.description: Apple just revealed a new brand identity for Apple Music, with the expected turn to Liquid Glass. I’m not much of a fan of their new design language in general; this is where I admit that I’m still running MacOS Sequoia and have grumpy things to say about rounded corner radii and text legibility. It’s just a trend, it will pass, and at some point I’ll probably cave and upgrade when it starts actually affecting my ability to get work done, or more importantly get security updates. Once I adjust, I’ll stop noticing it, and life will go on. As such, I wouldn’t normally find an obvious rebrand like this notable, much less feel like I had much to say about it. But then I happened to catch Apple’s behind-the-scenes video in my YouTube recommendations, and I realized I did have thoughts. Read full article Comments

item.title: Putin agrees to resume three-way talks with Kyiv and Washington

item.title: Osas Ighodaro Looks Like a Work of Art in This Blue Mosaic Gown by House of Marvee
item.description: Osas Ighodaro standing in her custom thermal-mapped blue mosaic gown by House of Marvee. If these photos of Osas Ighodaro have you staring at your screen a little longer than usual, we completely understand. Because how do you look at a dress this beautiful and simply scroll past? The colours, the design, the way it sits on her body! There’s so much to admire, and we’re right there with you. The Nigerian-American actor, host and producer has given us many reasons to love her fashion choices over the years, but this particular look has us especially curious about how it was made. Dressed in a gorgeous blue mosaic gown by House of Marvee, Osas looks like she stepped straight out of an art exhibition. And once you hear the inspiration behind the dress, you might appreciate it even more. Actor and host Osas Ighodaro wearing a blue mosaic gown crafted from hand-painted mother-of-pearl by House of Marvee. Here’s where it gets interesting. House of Marvee drew inspiration from thermal mapping, using different shades of blue to follow the natural curves of the body. The floor-length gown features hand-painted mother-of-pearl details, creating a mosaic effect that moves between deep ocean blues and brighter turquoise tones. Look closely, and you’ll notice how the colours and textures work together across the fabric. Osas Ighodaro posing in an asymmetrical one-shoulder blue mosaic dress featuring hand-painted mother-of-pearl tiles by House of Marvee. We also love how the one-shoulder design gives the dress room to shine. One arm is covered in a long sleeve, while the other shoulder is left bare, creating a lovely contrast. Osas keeps her accessories simple with gold hoop earrings, allowing the beautiful details of the gown to remain the focus. Osas Ighodaro posing in a House of Marvee hand-painted mother-of-pearl blue gown with gold hoop earrings and a finge And can we talk about her beauty look for a second? The retro finger waves, warm-toned makeup and gold hoop earrings complement those gorgeous shades of blue beautifully. From the hand-painted details to the way the gown follows her silhouette, House of Marvee has given us a dress we’d happily spend a few more minutes admiring. Osas Ighodaro lying down in a custom House of Marvee floor-length blue mosaic dress inside an art gallery space *** Photo Credit: House of Marvee/Instagram The post Osas Ighodaro Looks Like a Work of Art in This Blue Mosaic Gown by House of Marvee appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Trump exploits France riots to push false immigration claims ahead of midterms
item.description: Donald Trump and his inner circle are using unrest in France to push unsubstantiated claims blaming the riots on immigration, even showing French protest footage at midterm rallies. But there is no evidence linking immigration to the unrest, and it's prompted French President Emmanuel Macron to accuse world leaders of making “stupid comments” at France’s expense. Trump’s focus comes as Republicans face mounting pressure ahead of the midterms and his approval rating hits a reported record low.
item.dc:creator: Vedika BAHL
item.content:encoded: Donald Trump and his inner circle are using unrest in France to push unsubstantiated claims blaming the riots on immigration, even showing French protest footage at midterm rallies. But there is no evidence linking immigration to the unrest, and it's prompted French President Emmanuel Macron to accuse world leaders of making “stupid comments” at France’s expense. Trump’s focus comes as Republicans face mounting pressure ahead of the midterms and his approval rating hits a reported record low.

item.title: 'Neither the Sudanese military, nor the RSF take any acknowledgement of human life in this war'
item.description: The death toll from a drone strike Monday on a market in an area disputed between Sudan and South Sudan has risen to 153 and is likely even higher, a local official told AFP on Wednesday. Authorities in Abyei district said the strike on the Amiet market involved the use of multiple munitions and was carried out by the Sudanese army. FRANCE 24's Mark Owen speaks with Jan Pospisil, Sudan Affairs Analyst at the Peace and Conflict Resolution Evidence Platform. He says that for a long time the Sudanese army has tried "to portray a picture internationally that they are humane, whereas RSF is committing atrocities. Here we see very clearly that there is not much difference between these two".

item.title: People are vibe coding copyrighted apps with AI – will tech firms sue?
item.description: AI lets us remake software as we like Dmytro Olegovich Zakharchuk / Alamy Stock Photo I am waging a silent rebellion against Amazon. The internet giant owns Goodreads, the leading service for tracking and cataloguing books, but is generally considered to be a poor steward of the platform, which is built on ageing technology. Frustrated with the user experience, I have used AI to vibe code my own Goodreads app, relegating the official one to mere plumbing in my private fiefdom. Take that, Amazon, for I have breached your terms of service! I am not alone in my AI-enabled rebellion. It feels like I come across daily examples of people using AI to unofficially remix and remake software, whether that is creating a free copycat version of Adobe Photoshop , stripping the ads from their smart TV , mashing up video games or getting printers working on unsupported devices . It is all happening so quickly that lawyers don’t seem to have sprung into action to prevent it, though in some of the more egregious copyright-infringing cases, I would expect them to eventually. Read more Self-replicating AIs are a great digital horror story – here’s the reality For my Goodreads app, Amazon probably doesn’t know, or even care, about what I am doing. I won’t bore you with the full technical details, but I have built the app in such a way that it avoids mass “scraping” Goodreads – systematically harvesting data from its website – which would be easy to detect and block. By treading lightly, my app aims to resemble a human user and fly under the radar. Advertisement This connects to another ongoing battle over the interaction between AI-enabled individuals and companies: AI agents. The promise of an AI agent is that it can go out on to the internet and do things for you, like shopping or booking appointments. A flurry of examples has launched recently, including Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, and companies have begun fighting back, with the likes of Amazon and JPMorgan Chase blocking Muse in high-profile pushbacks. Ironically, Meta sits on both sides of this battle: its automated tools blocked a protest account on Instagram after detecting activity from a Claude AI tool that “resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems”. All of this comes down to a much older conundrum: where do your rights end and others’ begin? We have seen this play out every time a major new technology has hit the internet, and the results of a few historical examples might inform what happens next with AI. The first is a technology you probably don’t even think about anymore: your web browser. In the late 1990s, the two main browsers were Microsoft’s Internet Explorer and Netscape’s Navigator. They worked slightly differently, and websites often instructed users to choose one over the other. item.dc:creator: Jacob Aron
item.content:encoded: AI lets us remake software as we like Dmytro Olegovich Zakharchuk / Alamy Stock Photo I am waging a silent rebellion against Amazon. The internet giant owns Goodreads, the leading service for tracking and cataloguing books, but is generally considered to be a poor steward of the platform, which is built on ageing technology. Frustrated with the user experience, I have used AI to vibe code my own Goodreads app, relegating the official one to mere plumbing in my private fiefdom. Take that, Amazon, for I have breached your terms of service! I am not alone in my AI-enabled rebellion. It feels like I come across daily examples of people using AI to unofficially remix and remake software, whether that is creating a free copycat version of Adobe Photoshop , stripping the ads from their smart TV , mashing up video games or getting printers working on unsupported devices . It is all happening so quickly that lawyers don’t seem to have sprung into action to prevent it, though in some of the more egregious copyright-infringing cases, I would expect them to eventually. Read more Self-replicating AIs are a great digital horror story – here’s the reality For my Goodreads app, Amazon probably doesn’t know, or even care, about what I am doing. I won’t bore you with the full technical details, but I have built the app in such a way that it avoids mass “scraping” Goodreads – systematically harvesting data from its website – which would be easy to detect and block. By treading lightly, my app aims to resemble a human user and fly under the radar. Advertisement This connects to another ongoing battle over the interaction between AI-enabled individuals and companies: AI agents. The promise of an AI agent is that it can go out on to the internet and do things for you, like shopping or booking appointments. A flurry of examples has launched recently, including Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, and companies have begun fighting back, with the likes of Amazon and JPMorgan Chase blocking Muse in high-profile pushbacks. Ironically, Meta sits on both sides of this battle: its automated tools blocked a protest account on Instagram after detecting activity from a Claude AI tool that “resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems”. All of this comes down to a much older conundrum: where do your rights end and others’ begin? We have seen this play out every time a major new technology has hit the internet, and the results of a few historical examples might inform what happens next with AI. The first is a technology you probably don’t even think about anymore: your web browser. In the late 1990s, the two main browsers were Microsoft’s Internet Explorer and Netscape’s Navigator. They worked slightly differently, and websites often instructed users to choose one over the other. As more browsers flourished, Microsoft pushed back, most notably in 2003 by blocking a competitor browser called Opera from accessing its MSN website, a popular destination at the time. In the end, browsers began misidentifying themselves to websites as other browsers in an effort to avoid this. Today, the right to use any browser you like has essentially won out against the right of websites to restrict them, although the rise of dedicated smartphone apps has put some of the power back in companies’ hands. Nested within this battle was another: ad blockers. Once your browser has fetched the HTML code for a website, should you be obligated to display it all on your screen? As websites began displaying adverts to make money, people began downloading ad blocker add-ons to take back control of their browser. In response, companies developed new techniques for displaying ads, and ad blockers adjusted to remove them. Today there is a stalemate, with around 30 per cent of internet users blocking ads . Finally, there is the grandfather of all internet copyright battles: Napster, a peer-to-peer file-sharing service that people used to illegally share music files . The companies mostly won this battle thanks to the rise of Spotify and other similar music streaming services – with an easy legal option, piracy faded away, the side effect being that most people generally don’t own the music they listen to anymore. Internet users largely prevailed after the browser wars, ad blocking is at an impasse and streaming music seems to have benefitted the big corporations. What does all of this mean for AI? The difference here is decentralisation: just as I have used AI to create my own Goodreads app, so could anyone else, each of them slightly different. Fully blocking them all without restricting normal human access would be a monumental task. There is a slight caveat here – most AI use is centralised through the big providers like OpenAI and Anthropic, and Amazon could theoretically ask them to build in a block against creating such software (or sue them), but I think that is unlikely. In any case, the availability of open-weight AI models that anyone can download and run on their own hardware makes that a losing battle. I think it is most likely that we will be heading for a mix of all three. When it comes to remixing software, anything you do in the privacy of your own computer is going to be very hard to stop. Once you release it online, however, expect the lawyers to hunt you down. What we might see is the sharing of prompts that will get an AI to do the work for you in private – writing “recreate Photoshop, make no mistakes” isn’t something that any lawyer can stop – and there already exists a slightly more complicated version of this in the form of an instruction set for AI called Reverse Engineer Anything . As with browsers, individual choice will win, but this time the choices will be even more granular. Read more Hannah Fry: ‘AI can do some superhuman things – but so can forklifts’ For software that goes out into the wider internet, including AI agents, there will be two tiers. I expect Meta and Amazon will eventually come to some kind of agreement that allows Muse to shop for you. We are already seeing this with the development of a “personal agent protocol” that Meta is developing with businesses, including payment-processing services like Shopify and Stripe . For anyone using a commercial AI agent, what you can and can’t do will be decided by the companies, just as music streaming services dictate how you listen. But why should you use a commercial AI agent? People like me with a little technical know-how and even less coding ability are already using AI to create their own independent agents. As AI gets better at writing software, the barrier to entry will get lower and lower. I think companies will just have to come to accept this, as they have done with ad blockers. In future, a decent percentage of users that look like humans will actually be custom-made bots in disguise, doing things solely for the benefit of their creator. These bots will be ungovernable, for good and for ill. Further AI reading Anthropic has used its Claude AI model to solve a historical cryptography mystery . In the 1990s, the US National Security Agency (NSA) chose five specific mathematical objects called elliptic curves to serve as the basis for a cryptography standard used to generate digital signatures, now known as ECDSA. No one knew how these curves were chosen, but cryptography lore suggests that an NSA employee used a specific phrase , perhaps “Jerry deserves a raise”, to generate them. In fact, Claude was able to guess the specific mechanism – random number generation based on a timestamp – and regenerate the curves. The finding has no implications for cybersecurity, it merely answers a long-running question. Spotify says it has removed 50 million AI “slop and spam” tracks from recommendations on the platform, as part of a range of efforts to put “human artistry first”, according to the firm’s announcement. item.title: RIP BioWare: EA shuts down storied RPG studio after over three decades
item.description: The legendary studio behind series like Mass Effect , Dragon Age , Neverwinter Nights , and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is no more. BioWare announced via social media Wednesday afternoon that "after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending." The official announcement was posted mere minutes after a Bloomberg report detailed 400 job cuts across BioWare parent company Electronic Arts, including 50 at BioWare, based on reports from "a person familiar with the company's plans." "Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," EA executives wrote in a message to staff, according to Bloomberg. Read full article Comments

item.title: Nvidia woos wary Europeans with more open weights models
item.description: Nvidia hopes to capitalize on European sovereign AI demand by unloading a slew of new open weights models spanning chatbots, healthcare, and robotics. The major model devs have the resources to build highly capable models from scratch. But most enterprises don't, and have instead been forced to fine tune open weights models from the likes of Mistral or H Company using their own datasets. At GTC Berlin, Nvidia unveiled its latest additions to its open weights model library with refreshed Nemotron Retriever embedding and Alpamayo autonomous vehicle models. The point of embedding models While by no means the sexiest subclass of models out there, embedding models are some of the more useful ones for enterprise apps. Retrieval augmented generation (RAG), a technology we've explored extensively in the past, relies heavily on the embeddings generated by these models for applications like AI-augmented search. At a high level, RAG works by cutting up documentation in chunks, then converting those into vectors called embeddings. The embeddings are then ranked based on their relevance to the user's query before they're fed into an LLM's context. Nvidia's latest embedding and reranking models, based on Nemotron 3.5, support embeddings of both images and text across 34 languages. This time around, the models are being offered in sizes ranging from one to eight billion parameters, with NVFP4-quantized versions for those running on new Blackwell-based accelerators. That's small enough to run on something like a DGX Spark with plenty of room to spare for other models. Always take vendor claims with the usual grain of salt, but among competing embedding models, Nvidia boasts that at BF16-precision, its new 8 billion parameter embedding and reranking models are now the top-ranked dense models on the ViDoRe V3.1 benchmarks. However, not all documents are easily converted into embeddings. PDFs are notoriously difficult for embedding models to make sense of. They're often scanned from printed source material and formatted for consumption, which means scraping text and parsing charts. For this, Nvidia has also launched a refreshed Nemotron Parse model that's been trained specifically to extract information from PDF documents. Nvidia claims the model can process roughly 10.5 pages a second when running the one billion-parameter model on a single H100. Alongside the new embedding models, Nvidia is also rolling out access to Alpamayo 2 Edge, a more compact version of its autonomous driving model based on which promises real-time processing of streaming video and sensor data when running on the company's DRIVE AGX Thor platform. The models come just a week after the GPU giant launched its Nemotron 3.5 Super vision language (VL) model and teased Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, a 74 billion-parameter mixture of experts (MoE) model designed to fit in as little as 24 GB of video memory. That model, Nvidia says, will be available for download starting Friday. While open models provide ente

item.content:encoded: Nvidia hopes to capitalize on European sovereign AI demand by unloading a slew of new open weights models spanning chatbots, healthcare, and robotics. The major model devs have the resources to build highly capable models from scratch. At GTC Berlin, Nvidia unveiled its latest additions to its open weights model library with refreshed Nemotron Retriever embedding and Alpamayo autonomous vehicle models. The point of embedding models While by no means the sexiest subclass of models out there, embedding models are some of the more useful ones for enterprise apps. Retrieval augmented generation (RAG), a technology we've explored extensively in the past, relies heavily on the embeddings generated by these models for applications like AI-augmented search. At a high level, RAG works by cutting up documentation in chunks, then converting those into vectors called embeddings. The embeddings are then ranked based on their relevance to the user's query before they're fed into an LLM's context. Nvidia's latest embedding and reranking models, based on Nemotron 3.5, support embeddings of both images and text across 34 languages. This time around, the models are being offered in sizes ranging from one to eight billion parameters, with NVFP4-quantized versions for those running on new Blackwell-based accelerators. That's small enough to run on something like a DGX Spark with plenty of room to spare for other models. Always take vendor claims with the usual grain of salt, but among competing embedding models, Nvidia boasts that at BF16-precision, its new 8 billion parameter embedding and reranking models are now the top-ranked dense models on the ViDoRe V3.1 benchmarks. However, not all documents are easily converted into embeddings. PDFs are notoriously difficult for embedding models to make sense of. They're often scanned from printed source material and formatted for consumption, which means scraping text and parsing charts. For this, Nvidia has also launched a refreshed Nemotron Parse model that's been trained specifically to extract information from PDF documents. Nvidia claims the model can process roughly 10.5 pages a second when running the one billion-parameter model on a single H100. Alongside the new embedding models, Nvidia is also rolling out access to Alpamayo 2 Edge, a more compact version of its autonomous driving model based on which promises real-time processing of streaming video and sensor data when running on the company's DRIVE AGX Thor platform. The models come just a week after the GPU giant launched its Nemotron 3.5 Super vision language (VL) model and teased Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, a 74 billion-parameter mixture of experts (MoE) model designed to fit in as little as 24 GB of video memory. That model, Nvidia says, will be available for download starting Friday. While open models provide enterprises and governments a path toward sovereign AI, Nvidia's models are somewhat unique in how they're released. Most open weights models are a sort of black box. Anyone can download them, but the data and processes used to arrive at those weights is a mystery. This isn't the case with many of Nvidia's models: Alongside their weights, Nvidia routinely releases the training data and the recipes used to turn it into the final model. This means customers can not only inspect the model at a low level, but build a fully custom model based on Nvidia's Nemotron architecture, rather than trying to modify the weights after the fact through fine tuning. We should note that Nvidia is not the only one to do this. The Allen Institute has employed a similar strategy with its OLMo models for this very reason. ®

item.title: OpenAI's latest AI models are coming to Google Cloud and Antigravity
item.description: Google would certainly prefer that everyone used its Gemini models with Google Cloud services, but soon, you'll have more options. OpenAI and Google have come to an arrangement that will see the former's frontier models arrive in Google Cloud services. Perhaps more importantly, GPT models will soon appear in Antigravity, Google's agent-powered coding tool. For enterprise customers and AI enthusiasts, OpenAI's latest model will appear in Google's "Model Garden" in the coming weeks, adding to its 200-plus options. The garden already offers access to Google's Gemini models, as well as an assortment of open models like Mistral, Llama, and Gemma. Anthropic's Claude AI has also been available for some time. Google says it's now the only large cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed LLMs. While OpenAI notes that Microsoft continues to be its primary cloud partner, the full suite of current GPT 6 and 6.1 models—Astra, Sol, and Luna—will launch on Google Cloud. Astra will naturally cost the most to run, but Google's system supports dynamically moving workloads between LLMs based on performance, latency, and efficiency. Read full article Comments

item.title: NASA JPL Looks to Next 90 Years of Innovation, Exploration
item.description: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Clockwise from top: Caltech graduate students and friends carry out their first rocket firing on Halloween, 1936, in a dry riverbed along which JPL would rise. Their work helped make possible missions such as Perseverance and Europa Clipper as well as the future SkyFall and MoonFall missions. NASA/JPL-Caltech Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars. When a group of Caltech graduate students and enthusiasts began conducting rocket-propulsion tests in Pasadena’s Arroyo Seco on Oct. 31, 1936, they had no idea that their work marked the inception of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, the lab, now managed by Caltech for NASA, isn’t only celebrating the long line of historic firsts accomplished here; it’s paving the way for many to come. Initially a contractor for the U.S. Army, JPL launched America’s first satellite, Explorer 1 in 1958. But rather than just orbiting Earth like the Soviet Union’s Sputnik, Explorer 1 became the first spacecraft to conduct science, thanks to an onboard Geiger counter that discovered the protective radiation belts encircling Earth. The lab joined part of the newly formed NASA that same year. Within six years, in 1964, JPL sent the first U.S. mission to the Moon, Ranger 7 . It also went on to lead the first planetary flyby, the first probe to visit all four gas giants, the first infrared telescope, the first rovers to roll on Mars, and the first rotorcraft to fly there, among many other historic milestones. More firsts are on the way. “Over the course of 90 years, JPL’s first-of-a-kind missions have transformed our understanding of the universe and our place in it,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL’s director since 2025. In 1992, only a couple years after he started as an engineer at the lab, Gallagher led the JPL team that built and tested the Wide-Field and Planetary 2 Camera for NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, which delivered many of the mission’s most iconic images. “We stand on an extraordinary foundation, and we’re ready to push the boundaries with exciting new missions so that future generations can go even further.” Aiming for a 2028 launch, the JPL-managed SkyFall mission will deploy three helicopters mid-descent over Mars to search to map hidden ice deposits and analyze weather patterns. Helping advance NASA’s Moon Base, JPL is developing MoonFall , a mission that will land a group of large propulsive drones at the lunar South Pole that same year. Set for a 2027 launch, SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) features six toaster-oven-size satellites that will fly in formation to create a miles-wide radio antenna dish in order to study the Sun’s activity. What it reveals could help make space exploration safer for humans. Protecting humanity is also the goal of the asteroid-hunting NEO Surveyor (Near-Earth Object Surveyor) mission, which, managed by JPL, will hunt for potentially hazardous space rocks
item.dc:creator: Amanda Barnett
item.content:encoded: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Clockwise from top: Caltech graduate students and friends carry out their first rocket firing on Halloween, 1936, in a dry riverbed along which JPL would rise. Their work helped make possible missions such as Perseverance and Europa Clipper as well as the future SkyFall and MoonFall missions. NASA/JPL-Caltech Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars. When a group of Caltech graduate students and enthusiasts began conducting rocket-propulsion tests in Pasadena’s Arroyo Seco on Oct. 31, 1936, they had no idea that their work marked the inception of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, the lab, now managed by Caltech for NASA, isn’t only celebrating the long line of historic firsts accomplished here; it’s paving the way for many to come. Initially a contractor for the U.S. Army, JPL launched America’s first satellite, Explorer 1 in 1958. But rather than just orbiting Earth like the Soviet Union’s Sputnik, Explorer 1 became the first spacecraft to conduct science, thanks to an onboard Geiger counter that discovered the protective radiation belts encircling Earth. The lab joined part of the newly formed NASA that same year. Within six years, in 1964, JPL sent the first U.S. mission to the Moon, Ranger 7 . It also went on to lead the first planetary flyby, the first probe to visit all four gas giants, the first infrared telescope, the first rovers to roll on Mars, and the first rotorcraft to fly there, among many other historic milestones. More firsts are on the way. “Over the course of 90 years, JPL’s first-of-a-kind missions have transformed our understanding of the universe and our place in it,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL’s director since 2025. In 1992, only a couple years after he started as an engineer at the lab, Gallagher led the JPL team that built and tested the Wide-Field and Planetary 2 Camera for NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, which delivered many of the mission’s most iconic images. “We stand on an extraordinary foundation, and we’re ready to push the boundaries with exciting new missions so that future generations can go even further.” Aiming for a 2028 launch, the JPL-managed SkyFall mission will deploy three helicopters mid-descent over Mars to search to map hidden ice deposits and analyze weather patterns. Helping advance NASA’s Moon Base, JPL is developing MoonFall , a mission that will land a group of large propulsive drones at the lunar South Pole that same year. Set for a 2027 launch, SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) features six toaster-oven-size satellites that will fly in formation to create a miles-wide radio antenna dish in order to study the Sun’s activity. What it reveals could help make space exploration safer for humans. Protecting humanity is also the goal of the asteroid-hunting NEO Surveyor (Near-Earth Object Surveyor) mission, which, managed by JPL, will hunt for potentially hazardous space rocks that other telescopes can’t find. Once an object is spotted, NASA can offer a threat assessment and plan accordingly. Closer to home, the same lab that launched the first oceanographic satellite in 1978 is at work on several missions that will offer a deeper reading of Earth’s vital signs. Where one mission will monitor the movement of water by measuring slight changes in gravity, another will study how powerful tropical convective storms form. A third will detail how different types of air pollution affect human health. They add to a fleet of other Earth missions and projects JPL helps lead, including NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) a joint mission with the Indian Space Research Organisation that can pinpoint how Earth’s surface changes in relation to natural disasters. Another, one of a series of instruments called AVIRIS (Airborne Visible Infrared Imaging Spectrometer), can even detect rare Earth elements critical to modern technology. Flown on airplanes, the AVIRIS sensors were developed at JPL’s Microdevices Laboratory , which invented the “camera on a chip” technology that enables cellphones to take pictures. It’s also where the detectors are being developed for PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), a newly announced NASA mission that will strengthen humanity’s understanding of the universe by studying radiant energy visible only in the far-infrared. “Bringing together the very best of scientific brilliance and engineering ingenuity from across Caltech and JPL continues to advance NASA’s priorities and empower America’s space leadership,” said Caltech’s president Ray Jayawardhana, who is also a professor of astronomy. “I can only imagine what those Caltech students experimenting with rockets in a little patch of dry riverbed would think if they could to see what Caltech and JPL have accomplished since, and where we’re headed next. Ninety years later, the same spirit of daring is still opening new frontiers and inspiring humanity.” The 90th anniversary comes just a few weeks before another milestone, when on Nov. 18 Voyager 1 reaches a full light-day — the distance light will travel in 24 hours, which is some 16 billion miles, or 26 billion kilometers — from Earth. Ed Stone led the mission for 50 years, serving as JPL’s director for 10 of them. Stone died in 2024, but the Voyagers are continuing on their journey deeper into interstellar space, a place no other spacecraft have ventured. Turning 50 next year, they rely on NASA’s Deep Space Network (developed by JPL in the Apollo era) to receive commands and send back science data. Stone said that with both Voyagers exploring regions never before visited, “every day is a day of discovery.” The same could be said for JPL. -end- Media contact Matthew Segal Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif. 818-354-8307 matthew.j.segal@jpl.nasa.gov 2026-073 Share Details Last Updated Oct 21, 2026 Related Terms Jet Propulsion Laboratory Explore More 6 min read NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system… Article 7 days ago 4 min read NASA JPL Testing Readies Voyager Technologies Lander for Moon Mission Article 1 week ago 5 min read NASA’s SPHEREx Telescope Sees Menagerie of Brown Dwarfs Article 2 weeks ago Keep Exploring Discover More Topics From NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory Europa Clipper SkyFall NASA’s SkyFall mission to Mars, building on the success of the Ingenuity helicopter, will send a trio of aircraft to… Mars Perseverance Rover The Mars Perseverance rover is the first leg the Mars Sample Return Campaign’s interplanetary relay team. item.title: Report: Musk ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, then blamed it on Trump
item.description: A Wall Street Journal report said SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered the Starlink throttling that blindsided Ukraine's air assault forces last week, despite Musk's claim that all decisions on the military version of Starlink are made by the US military and President Trump. Trump denied ordering the restrictions. While Musk may have spoken to Trump and administration officials before the decision, The Wall Street Journal reported yesterday that Musk made the final call. The decision came after both Musk and Trump criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries. "Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine, a decision that sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration," the WSJ wrote, citing unnamed US officials and people familiar with the matter. The report said that "Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network... rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless." Read full article Comments

item.title: LiteLLM supply chain attack hoovers up passwords and secrets
item.description: Unknown crims compromised LiteLLM's release process on Wednesday, distributing a malicious version (1.107.0) containing malware designed to steal cloud and AI credentials and a remote access trojan (RAT) capable of executing arbitrary code on infected machines through PyPI and Docker registries. PyPI quarantined the trojanized version of the popular open source AI gateway within hours, and the Docker image (litellm/litellm:1.107.0) was removed from both Docker Hub and GHCR soon after - but anyone who ran the compromised package on any platform should assume their secrets have been stolen. “Check for /tmp/.pc_once_* (the exfil has already fired if this file exists) and /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock (the C2 daemon ran or is still running if this file exists),” advised Aikido Security malware hunter Ilyas Makari. “The same applies to anyone who ran the official Docker image litellm/litellm:1.107.0 , or pulled it via the latest , main-latest , or main-stable tags.” The most recent safe version is v1.106.2. While it’s too early to tell the scale of this latest LiteLLM supply chain attack – an earlier LiteLLM compromise in March potentially exposed more than 2,500 organizations and 434,000 CI/CD pipelines worldwide, according to CloudSEK – make sure to take these measures seriously, and check environments for any indicators of compromise. Aikido, Google’s Wiz cloud security biz, and supply-chain security provider Socket have all published extensive threat-hunting and mitigation instructions for LiteLLM users and security teams, so give those a read stat. LiteLLM, developed by BerriAI, provides a common interface for LLM providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Gemini, and receives about 23 million weekly downloads. This means a compromised installation can run alongside LLM provider API keys, cloud identities, and database connection strings - and expose a ton of valuable credentials, secrets, and other sensitive data to whoever uploaded the malicious package. “Teams using 1.107.0 should stop deploying it and investigate environments where Python ran after installation, including proxy containers and CI runners,” Socket researchers said on Wednesday. The malicious version was uploaded at 11:39 UTC, and according to Wiz kids Benjamin Read and Rami McCarthy, the payload originates with malicious commits made on github.com/Berri-AI/litellm , which is a hyphenated variant of the legitimate BerriAI organization. Miscreants used this repo to inject the three malicious files into the LiteLLM release pipeline. These, according to Makari, include cook.pth , which causes the second file, cook.py , to run automatically every time Python is invoked on the machine, without any additional user action.
